The existing accounts of Febronia describe her as a young woman who remained faithful to Christ in the face of persecution. While specific narratives about her interrogations and sufferings come from later legendary material rather than reliable contemporary sources, the core witness attributed to her is that of a virgin who gave her life rather than renounce her Christian faith. This witness, whatever the historical details, is the reason she has been honored as a martyr.

Febronia is remembered as a patron of martyrs and of young women, reflecting both the manner of her death and the example of fidelity she represents. Her feast day is celebrated on February 16, and she continues to be invoked by the faithful as a model of courage and purity. Her enduring presence in the sanctoral cycle stands as a testament to the lasting resonance of her story within Catholic devotion, even where the historical particulars remain uncertain.

biography: Saint Felicity was an enslaved woman living in the Roman province of Africa during the early third century. Her name appears alongside that of her mistress, the young catechumen Vibia Perpetua, in one of the most celebrated documents of early Christianity: the Passion of Perpetua and Felicity. Felicity's presence in this account, written by contemporaries of the events, is significant because it gave voice and visibility to an enslaved woman at a moment when such persons were otherwise largely excluded from the historical record.

Felicity and Perpetua were arrested in Carthage around the year 203, during the persecution of Christians under the Roman emperor Septimius Severus. They were part of a small group of catechumens that also included the free men Saturninus, Secundulus, and Saturus. According to the Passion, Felicity was eight months pregnant at the time of her arrest, which posed an immediate legal complication: Roman law prohibited the execution of pregnant women, and Felicity feared she would be separated from her companions and left to die alone in prison after they had been martyred. Her fellow prisoners reportedly prayed on her behalf, and she gave birth to a daughter just a few days before the scheduled games. The child was later cared for by a Christian family.

The account of Felicity's martyrdom is preserved in her own words and in those of Perpetua. Felicity is recorded as saying, 'What I suffer now, I suffer alone. But then, another will be in me who will suffer for me,' words that have become one of the most quoted reflections on Christian endurance. She and Perpetua were scourged before being sent into the amphitheater. According to the Passion, Perpetua was tossed by a wild cow, and Felicity, at Perpetua's request, was also exposed to the animal. After this, the two women were led back into the arena where, along with the others, they were killed by the sword. Perpetua guided the gladiator's hand to her own throat.

The account is generally believed to have been edited and prefaced by the North African theologian Tertullian, though the actual narrative portions were written by Perpetua, Felicity, and Saturus themselves. The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity has been treasured for centuries as one of the few early Christian texts authored in part by women and slaves, and it remains an important witness to the experience of early martyrs. Felicity's name was added to the Roman Canon of the Mass by the seventh century, an unusual honor that secured her place in the Church's universal liturgical memory.

Felicity is venerated as a patron of expectant mothers, of women who struggle with barrenness, and of parents who have lost children, patronages that grew directly from the circumstances of her imprisonment and martyrdom. Her feast day is celebrated on March 7, traditionally shared with Perpetua. The two saints are typically depicted together in Christian art, often shown as young women in chains or in the arena, and their story has been a touchstone for Christian reflection on suffering, courage, and the dignity of every human person regardless of social status.

faqs.question: Who was Saint Felicity of Carthage?
faqs.answer: Saint Felicity was an enslaved woman in early third-century Carthage who was arrested for her Christian faith and martyred in the arena in 203 alongside her mistress, Saint Perpetua. Her own words and those of her companions are preserved in the famous Passion of Perpetua and Felicity.

The text is notable for giving direct voice to women and an enslaved person in early Christian literature.

biography:
Felipe de Jesús de las Casas was born around 1572 in Mexico City, then part of the Viceroyalty of New Spain. He grew up in a family with a tradition of civic and religious life; his father is sometimes identified as a physician. As a young man, Felipe was known for a restless and somewhat worldly temperament, and he left home at least once to travel to the Philippines, apparently with uncertain motives. After an early attempt to enter religious life did not take, he eventually joined the Franciscan Order, reportedly while still in Manila, and was professed as a friar in the Order of Friars Minor. He later returned briefly to Mexico before heading back to the Philippines to continue his formation.

In late 1596, Felipe set sail from Manila aboard the San Felipe as part of a Spanish trading expedition bound for Mexico. According to Franciscan and Japanese accounts, a severe storm drove the ship off course and it put in at the port of Shiki (Urado) on the Japanese island of Shikoku. There, the arrogant behavior of the pilot and the cargo's commercial value attracted the attention of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, the ruler of a Japan increasingly hostile to Christianity. Hideyoshi accused the friars of being spies for an imagined Christian invasion, and he ordered the execution of those aboard who were in religious life.

Along with Franciscan confreres, a Dominican, and Japanese catechists and lay faithful, Felipe was arrested, subjected to a forced march across Japan, and brought to Nagasaki in early 1597. On February 5, 1597, he and the others were crucified on a hillside in Nagasaki, in an event that became known as the Twenty-Six Martyrs of Japan. Felipe was the youngest of the Franciscan friars among the group, and tradition identifies him as the one who preached briefly to the crowd from the cross. Their deaths, witnessed by a large number of Christians, were reported in letters written by survivors and later sent to the Franciscan and Dominican provinces in the Philippines and Mexico.

Felipe and his companions were beatified by Pope Urban VIII in 1627 and canonized by Pope Pius IX on June 8, 1862. The Twenty-Six Martyrs of Japan are commemorated jointly on February 5 in the General Roman Calendar. In Mexico, Felipe is honored as the country's first native-born saint, and he is widely invoked as a patron of Mexico City, where a major thoroughfare and parish bear his name. A persistent legend holds that a dried fig tree in his family's Mexico City home reportedly bloomed on the day of his martyrdom, a story passed down in hagiographic tradition though difficult to verify independently. His brief life and sudden death in a foreign land made him a symbol of the missionary reach of the early Catholic Church from the New World to Asia.

faqs.answer: He was arrested in Japan after a Spanish ship was driven off course, and he was crucified in Nagasaki on February 5, 1597, alongside twenty-five other Christians, including Franciscans, a Dominican, and Japanese lay faithful.

faqs.answer: The ruler Toyotomi Hideyoshi was persecuting Christians in Japan and accused the friars of being agents of a foreign invasion, which led to the order for their execution.
