The order took its name and inspiration from St. Francis de Sales, the gentle Bishop of Geneva known for his pastoral approach. A year later, in 1872, Bosco co-founded the Institute of the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians with St. Mary Mazzarello, bringing the Salesian educational mission to girls as well. He developed a distinctive method of education that combined reason, religion, and loving kindness, a system he called the 'Preventive System,' which sought to form the whole person rather than rely on fear or punishment. He was also a prolific writer and publisher, founding Catholic publishing houses and reading societies, which is why he is counted among the patron saints of editors.

Bosco's work drew strong support from the papacy. Pope Pius IX, who became pope in 1846, backed Bosco's expanding projects with encouragement and approval as the Salesians grew. Bosco also launched missions abroad on his initiative, most famously sending groups of Salesian missionaries to Patagonia in 1875 to evangelize among the indigenous peoples and Italian immigrants there, while he himself remained in Turin directing the work. In his final years, declining health forced him to slow down, but he continued to write, preach, and direct the Society. He died in the early hours of January 31, 1888, at the Oratory in Valdocco, Turin, surrounded by his Salesian community. He was canonized by Pope Pius XI in 1934 and later declared 'Father and Teacher of Youth' by Pope John Paul II in 1989.

Bosco's legacy lives on through the Salesian family, which today counts thousands of members working in schools, youth centers, parishes, and missions on every inhabited continent. The Salesians continue his educational approach, and shrines like the Basilica of Mary Help of Christians in Turin, which Bosco himself promoted, remain major pilgrimage sites. He is also remembered for his reputed gift of working with the young and for his affection for the 'tricks and illusions' he used to draw children into his oratories, including sleight-of-hand and early cinema screenings, a love that led to his patronage of magicians.

faqs.question: Who is St. John Bosco?
faqs.answer: St. John Bosco (1815-1888) was an Italian Catholic priest from Piedmont who dedicated his life to the education and spiritual care of poor and abandoned young people. He founded the Salesians of Don Bosco, one of the largest religious orders in the Catholic Church.

faqs.question: When is St. John Bosco's feast day?
faqs.answer: St. John Bosco's feast day is celebrated on January 31, the date of his death in 1888 in Turin.

faqs.question: What is St. John Bosco the patron saint of?
faqs.answer: He is the patron saint of youth, students, editors, apprentices, and magicians. He was also declared 'Father and Teacher of Youth' by Pope John Paul II in 1989.

faqs.question: What did St. John Bosco do?
faqs.answer: He founded the Salesians of Don Bosco in 1859, a religious order devoted to educating and caring for underprivileged young people. He also co-founded the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians, established schools and publishing houses, and pioneered a gentle, reason-based approach to education called the Preventive System.

faqs.question: Why is St. John Bosco associated with magic tricks?
faqs.answer: Bosco used sleight-of-hand tricks, acrobatics, and later magic lantern shows to attract children to his oratories, where he could then teach them catechism and life skills. This lifelong love of stage performance and illusion is the traditional reason he is named a patron of magicians.

faqs.question: Where was St. John Bosco born and where did he live?
faqs.answer: He was born in 1815 in Castelnuovo Don Bosco, a small village near Turin in northern Italy, and spent most of his priestly life and ministry in the city of Turin, especially at the Oratory of Valdocco.

biography:
St. John Cantius (Jan Kanty in Polish) was born in 1390 in Kęty, a small town in the region of Lesser Poland. Details of his early life are not abundant, but he came from a modest family and demonstrated an early aptitude for learning and piety. He pursued his studies at the University of Kraków, the intellectual heart of medieval Poland, where he eventually earned a doctorate in theology. The university environment shaped him profoundly, and he was known even as a young man for combining scholarly rigor with genuine devotion.

After completing his formation, John was ordained a priest and joined the faculty of the University of Kraków, where he became a professor of theology. He is said to have taught at the university for several decades, and he later served as rector of the institution — a notable distinction for any scholar, let alone one known for his humility. His academic career coincided with the early years of St. John of Kenty, a contemporary at the university, though careful scholarship is needed to separate fact from the many pious legends that accumulated around him. His lectures reportedly drew large numbers of students, and he was known for his generosity toward the poor, often giving away much of what he had — including, according to tradition, his very clothes and shoes.

John's pastoral and charitable work extended beyond the lecture hall. He served as a parish priest in Olkusz for a time and was a devoted pilgrim, reportedly walking barefoot to Rome, Jerusalem, and other holy sites. His pilgrimages, if the traditional accounts are accurate, are striking examples of the physical austerities he embraced alongside his intellectual and pastoral life. He was a member of the Canons Regular of St. Augustine, a religious order committed to combining contemplation with ministry.

He died on December 24, 1473, in Kraków, after a life devoted to teaching, preaching, and charity. His tomb in the Church of St. Anne in Kraków became a place of veneration soon after his death. He was beatified by Pope Clement X in 1673, and was later canonized by Pope Clement XII in 1767 — a formal recognition of the holiness that his students and contemporaries had long observed in him.

Today, St. John Cantius is honored as the patron of students, educators, and teachers, and his feast day is celebrated on October 20. His example — a scholar who wore out his shoes walking to help the poor and to visit holy places — continues to inspire those who believe that the life of the mind and the life of charity are meant to be lived together. The University of Kraków, now known as the Jagiellonian University, still holds him in particular esteem as one of its most distinguished medieval figures.

faqs.question: Who is St. John Cantius?
faqs.answer: St. John Cantius (1390–1473) was a Polish priest, professor of theology, and member of the Canons Regular of St. Augustine. He is best known for his long career teaching at the University of Kraków and for his generosity to the poor.

faqs.question: When is St. John Cantius's feast day?
faqs.answer: His feast day is celebrated on October 20 in the Roman Catholic liturgical calendar.

faqs.question: What is St. John Cantius the patron saint of?
faqs.answer: He is the patron saint of students, educators, and teachers, reflecting his lifelong dedication to teaching and formation in the faith.

faqs.question: When was St. John Cantius canonized?
faqs.answer: He was canonized by Pope Clement XII in 1767, after having been beatified by Pope Clement X in 1673.

faqs.question: What did St. John Cantius do?
faqs.answer: He served as a theology professor and rector at the University of Kraków, worked as a parish priest, made pilgrimages to holy sites, and was famous for giving generously to the poor — reportedly even giving away his own clothing and shoes.

biography: John Chrysostom was born around 347 in Antioch, one of the great cities of the Roman Empire and an important center of early Christianity in what is now modern-day Turkey. He came from a Christian family; his father died when he was young, and he was raised primarily by his mother, Anthusa. He received an excellent classical education, studying rhetoric under the pagan rhetorician Libanius, and was preparing for a career in law or public speaking before his life took a different turn.

After his mother's death (or possibly her urging), John withdrew from public life and was baptized around 368. He spent several years as a monk in the mountains near Antioch, living an ascetic life so extreme that it permanently damaged his health. He later returned to the city and was ordained a deacon in 381 and a priest in 386 by Bishop Flavian of Antioch, whose trusted adviser he became.

It was as a priest in Antioch that John earned his enduring reputation. For roughly twelve years, he preached frequently and at length, drawing enormous crowds and earning the nickname "Chrysostom"—Greek for "golden-mouthed." His homilies, many of which survive today, included verse-by-verse commentary on Scripture (notably on Genesis, the Psalms, and the letters of Paul), as well as sermons on saints and on the proper Christian use of wealth. He was a sharp critic of extravagance among the rich and called repeatedly for care of the poor.

In 398, partly through the influence of the imperial court, John was made Archbishop of Constantinople. He launched a program of reform—overhauling the clergy, disciplining lax bishops, simplifying ecclesiastical life, and curbing the lavish spending of the imperial family, especially Empress Eudoxia. These efforts made powerful enemies, and in 403 he was deposed at a synod convened by Theophilus of Alexandria, an opponent he had earlier condemned. A few months later, after a popular uprising, he was briefly restored, but conflict with the court resumed, and he was exiled in 404. He never returned.

John was sent first to Cucusus in the mountains of Armenia and finally to Pityus on the eastern Black Sea coast. He died in transit in September 407, having reportedly been forced into an exhausting march. Although he was never formally tried on the specific charges brought against him, his reputation was rehabilitated within decades. The Eastern Church honors him as one of its great hierarchs, the West venerates him as a Doctor of the Church, and the "Divine Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom" remains the most commonly used Eucharistic liturgy in the Byzantine tradition today.

His legacy is complicated. He wrote beautiful passages on mercy and the poor, but he also left behind anti-Jewish homilies that modern readers rightly find troubling. He is remembered as a fearless preacher who suffered for confronting power, and as a pastor whose concern for the soul of the Christian community extended to those on its margins.

faqs.question: Who is St. John Chrysostom?
faqs.answer: St. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407) was an archbishop of Constantinople and one of the most celebrated preachers of the early Church. The nickname "Chrysostom," meaning "golden-mouthed," reflects his renowned eloquence.

faqs.question: What is St. John Chrysostom the patron saint of?
faqs.answer: He is a patron saint of preachers, the city of Constantinople, and people with epilepsy, among other groups associated with his ministry and intercessory tradition.

faqs.question: When is St. John Chrysostom's feast day?
faqs.answer: His feast day is September 13 in the Roman Catholic calendar. Eastern Christians also commemorate him on November 13 and January 27.

faqs.question: What did St. John Chrysostom do?
faqs.answer: He served as Archbishop of Constantinople from 398, preached extensively (leaving behind hundreds of homilies still read today), and pushed for reforms of clerical and imperial life that led to his exile and eventual death in 407.

faqs.question: Why is he called a Doctor of the Church?
faqs.answer: He is honored as a Doctor of the Church because of the depth, volume, and lasting influence of his preaching and theological writing, including the Eucharistic liturgy that bears his name in the Eastern Christian tradition.

faqs.question: How did St. John Chrysostom die?
faqs.answer: He died in September 407 while being moved into further exile on the eastern Black Sea coast, reportedly after a forced march that his frail health could not withstand.

biography: John Climacus was a 7th-century Christian monk whose exact birth date and early background are not well documented by historical sources. What is known is that as a young man, around the age of sixteen, he entered the Monastery of Saint Catherine at Mount Sinai, one of the oldest and most renowned monastic communities in the Christian world. This desert monastery, located at the foot of the mountain traditionally associated with Moses and the receiving of the Law, became the formative setting for his entire spiritual life.

After roughly nineteen years of community life and obedience under the guidance of an elder, John withdrew into a more solitary existence. He spent approximately forty years living as a hermit in a cave near the summit of Mount Sinai, dedicating himself to prayer, silence, and ascetic discipline. This extended period of solitude profoundly shaped his spiritual outlook, grounding his later teaching in direct experience of the contemplative life rather than purely theoretical reflection.

Around the year 640, the monks of Sinai elected him as abbot of their community, a position he held until shortly before his death. The transition from hermit to abbot marked a significant shift in his vocation, though he is said to have continued living an austere and prayerful life even in this leadership role. He is generally believed to have reposed around 649, though the precise year of his death is not recorded with certainty.

John is best known for his spiritual masterwork, The Ladder of Divine Ascent (Klimax tou Paradeisou), composed near the end of his life at the request of his fellow abbot, John of Raïthu. The work is structured as thirty steps or rungs, each addressing a particular spiritual discipline or obstacle to be overcome, beginning with renunciation of the world and culminating in theosis, or union with God. Drawn from Scripture, the Desert Fathers, and his own observation of monastic life, it became one of the most influential texts in Eastern Christian spirituality and is still read widely in Orthodox and Catholic monastic traditions.

His epithet 'Climacus,' meaning 'of the ladder' (from the Greek klimax), was given to him in reference to this work, rather than being a family name. The Ladder has remained required reading in Orthodox monasteries for centuries, and its teachings continue to shape Christian ascetical theology. John is commemorated in the Roman Catholic Church on March 30, while in the Eastern Orthodox tradition his feast is also observed on the Fourth Sunday of Great Lent, when The Ladder is read in its entirety in monasteries as part of the Lenten preparation.

faqs.question: Who is St. John Climacus?
faqs.answer: St. John Climacus was a 7th-century Christian monk and abbot at the Monastery of Saint Catherine on Mount Sinai, best known for authoring The Ladder of Divine Ascent, one of the most influential works of Christian ascetical literature.

faqs.question: When is St. John Climacus's feast day?
faqs.answer: In the Roman Catholic Church, his feast day is celebrated on March 30. In the Eastern Orthodox tradition, he is also commemorated on the Fourth Sunday of Great Lent.

faqs.question: What is St. John Climacus the patron saint of?
faqs.answer: He is regarded as a patron of those pursuing spiritual growth and of monastics, reflecting the ascetical focus of his teaching and his long life in the Sinai desert.

faqs.question: What is The Ladder of Divine Ascent?
faqs.answer: The Ladder of Divine Ascent is John Climacus's principal written work, organized as thirty 'rungs' or chapters that guide the reader through stages of spiritual discipline, from renunciation of worldly attachments to the heights of divine love.

faqs.question: Where did John Climacus live?
faqs.answer: He lived at the Monastery of Saint Catherine on the Sinai Peninsula in present-day Egypt, first as a monastic, then as a hermit in a nearby cave, and finally as abbot of the community.

faqs.question: Is St. John Climacus venerated in both Catholic and Orthodox traditions?
faqs.answer: Yes, he is recognized as a saint in both the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Churches, and The Ladder of Divine Ascent is read especially widely in Orthodox monastic life during Great Lent.

biography: Jean Eudes was born on November 14, 1601, in the small Norman town of Ri, France, the son of a farmer. He grew up in a region still marked by the religious wars of the previous century, and his early years were shaped by a strong Catholic faith nurtured at home and in the local parish. From a young age, he felt drawn to the priesthood, and he was eventually sent to the Jesuit college at Caen, where he received a solid humanistic and theological formation.

In 1623, Eudes joined the Oratory of Jesus and Mary in Paris, an association of secular priests founded by Pierre de Bérulle that emphasized spiritual formation and the renewal of the French clergy. It was among the Oratorians that he was ordained, around 1625, and he was soon sent to the diocese of Lisieux. There he preached parish missions, and in 1634 he helped found a congregation of women religious to care for women in difficult situations, a project that reflected his lifelong concern for those on the margins of society.

In 1643, Eudes left the Oratory to establish a new community, which led him to found the Congregation of Jesus and Mary, also known as the Eudists, in 1643 (some sources note 1643 or shortly after). The Eudists were dedicated to the formation of diocesan clergy through seminaries, a pressing need in a France where many priests were poorly trained. He also founded the Sisters of Our Lady of Charity of the Refuge to shelter women who had been driven to prostitution by poverty or coercion, an apostolate that cost him a great deal of energy in a country only beginning to recover from the upheavals of the Fronde. It is for this latter work that St. John Eudes is sometimes cited as a co-patron of those who work with survivors of exploitation, although that association is widely noted but not formally proclaimed by the Church.

Eudes' most lasting contribution to Catholic spirituality was the promotion of the devotion to the Sacred Hearts of Jesus and Mary. In 1672, he composed the Mass and Office of the Sacred Heart of Jesus, more than a year before the revelations to St. Margaret Mary Alacoque at Paray-le-Monial, and he is generally credited as the first to give this devotion a public liturgical expression. He was likewise the first to compose a Mass and Office in honor of the Heart of Mary. He wrote extensively on the interior life, including the devotional classic "The Life and Kingdom of Jesus," and he died at Caen on August 19, 1680, in the middle of a mission he was preaching.

John Eudes was beatified in 1909 and canonized by Pope Pius XI in 1925. He is honored as one of the great missionary preachers of seventeenth-century France, and his writings continue to nourish the spiritual life. His feast day is observed on August 19 in the current Roman calendar, and his Congregation of Jesus and Mary and the Sisters of Our Lady of Charity of the Refuge still carry on his work in many parts of the world.

faqs.question: Who is St. John Eudes?
faqs.answer: St. John Eudes (1601-1680) was a French priest, missionary, and founder of the Congregation of Jesus and Mary (the Eudists) and the Sisters of Our Lady of Charity of the Refuge. He is best known for his pioneering devotion to the Sacred Hearts of Jesus and Mary.

faqs.question: When is St. John Eudes' feast day?
faqs.answer: His feast day is celebrated on August 19, the anniversary of his death at Caen in 1680.

faqs.question: What is St. John Eudes the patron saint of?
faqs.answer: He is associated with the devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus and the Heart of Mary, and is often invoked for priests and for France. He is also sometimes cited for those who minister to people who have been exploited.

faqs.question: What did St. John Eudes do for the Sacred Heart devotion?
faqs.answer: He composed the first Mass and Office in honor of the Sacred Heart of Jesus in 1672, predating the revelations given to St. Margaret Mary Alacoque, and is generally credited as the first to give this devotion a public liturgical form.

faqs.question: What religious congregations did St. John Eudes found?
faqs.answer: He founded the Congregation of Jesus and Mary (the Eudists) in 1643, dedicated to the formation of diocesan clergy, and the Sisters of Our Lady of Charity of the Refuge, devoted to sheltering women in difficult circumstances.

faqs.question: Where can I learn more about St. John Eudes?
faqs.answer: Beyond the entries in the Catholic Encyclopedia and the Vatican, the Eudist Fathers maintain archives and biographical resources about his life, writings, and spiritual legacy.

biography: John Fisher was born in 1469 in Beverley, Yorkshire, into a family of modest means. His father, a prosperous merchant, died when John was still young, but his mother ensured he received a solid education. He studied at the collegiate church in Beverley before going on to Cambridge, where he was elected a fellow of St. John's College and eventually became its president. He was ordained a priest in 1491 and soon became one of the most respected scholars and preachers in England, eventually serving as Lady Margaret Beaufort's personal chaplain and confessor.

In 1504, Fisher was appointed Bishop of Rochester, a small and relatively poor diocese. Rather than see it as a step down, he embraced it as a vocation and served faithfully for the rest of his life. He also held the position of Chancellor of Cambridge University and used his influence to promote rigorous theological education. He is often credited with helping to found St. John's College, Cambridge, and he championed the work of humanist scholars including Erasmus, with whom he maintained a long correspondence. His learning, preaching, and personal austerity made him one of the most respected churchmen in England.

Fisher's life took a decisive turn when Henry VIII began his campaign to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon. The bishop had long been a trusted adviser to the queen, and he publicly defended the validity of her marriage and the pope's authority to rule on such matters. When Henry pushed through the Act of Supremacy, declaring himself head of the Church in England, Fisher was one of the few bishops who refused to swear the required oath. He also spoke out against the king's divorce and the subsequent break with Rome, believing the king's actions threatened the unity of the Church and the salvation of souls.

In 1535, Fisher was arrested and tried for treason after refusing to acknowledge Henry as Supreme Head of the Church. The king, reportedly angered that Pope Paul III had named Fisher a cardinal, reportedly said the pope could send him a hat, but he would have no head to wear it. Fisher was executed by beheading on June 22, 1535, dying with remarkable composure and reportedly uttering the words of the psalm, 'This is the glory of all the saints.' His head was placed on London Bridge, while his body was interred at the Church of St Peter ad Vincula within the Tower of London.

Fisher was beatified in 1886 by Pope Leo XIII and canonized in 1935 by Pope Pius XI alongside his fellow martyr Thomas More, four hundred years after their deaths. He is honored as a patron of bishops, theologians, and priests, and his feast day is observed on June 22, shared with St. Thomas More. His writings, including his spiritual meditations and treatises against Luther, remain valuable windows into the early English Reformation. He stands as a quiet but firm witness to the cost of conscience and the principle that no earthly authority can override the truths of the Christian faith.

faqs.question: Who is St. John Fisher?
faqs.answer: St. John Fisher was an English bishop, theologian, and chancellor of Cambridge University who opposed King Henry VIII's break with the Catholic Church. He was executed in 1535 and later canonized as a martyr.

faqs.question: What is St. John Fisher the patron saint of?
faqs.answer: He is venerated as a patron of bishops, theologians, and priests, reflecting his own roles as a scholarly bishop and defender of Church teaching.

faqs.question: When is St. John Fisher's feast day?
faqs.answer: His feast day is celebrated on June 22, which he shares with his fellow martyr St. Thomas More.

faqs.question: Why was St. John Fisher executed?
faqs.answer: He was executed for treason after refusing to accept Henry VIII as the Supreme Head of the Church of England and continuing to recognize the pope's authority.

faqs.question: Was St. John Fisher a cardinal?
faqs.answer: Yes. Pope Paul III appointed him a cardinal in 1535, while he was already imprisoned in the Tower of London, a gesture that reportedly angered Henry VIII.

faqs.question: Where is St. John Fisher buried?
faqs.answer: His body was interred at the Church of St Peter ad Vincula within the Tower of London, where his remains rest today.

biography:
John Francis Regis was born on January 31, 1597, in Fontcouverte, a village in the Languedoc region of southern France. He came from a prosperous merchant family with roots in the textile trade, and his father had served in local government. The family was devoutly Catholic, and the young John Francis grew up in a region where the religious landscape was complex — the aftermath of the Wars of Religion still lingered, and Jansenist ideas would soon begin to spread among the clergy. From an early age, he showed a strong inclination toward the priesthood and was known among his peers for his piety and seriousness of character.

He pursued his studies at the Jesuit college in Béziers and later at the University of Toulouse, where he was first exposed to the writings and spirituality of the Society of Jesus. In 1616, at the age of nineteen, he entered the Jesuit novitiate at Toulouse. The following years were marked by rigorous intellectual and spiritual formation. He was ordained a priest in 1631 and soon after was assigned to work among the rural poor, a mission that would define the rest of his short life. The years of his Jesuit formation coincided with a period in which Jansenism — with its austere and moral rigorism — was gaining ground in France, and Regis would later become a notable opponent of this heresy through his preaching.

Regis is best known for his missionary work in the countryside of southern France, particularly in the regions of Le Velay, Viviers, and the area around Toulouse. He often walked barefoot, sometimes through snow and harsh weather, to reach remote villages where many people had received little or no formal religious instruction. He preached with great directness, focused especially on three groups: the poor and marginalized, the indifferently Catholic who had drifted from practice, and those influenced by Jansenist or Protestant ideas. Beyond preaching, he established networks of charitable assistance, helped organize retreats, and reportedly worked to rescue women from difficult circumstances, including those caught in prostitution or exploitation — a risky apostolate that sometimes earned him the hostility of local interests. His physical stamina was remarkable, and he reportedly wore his body down over years of relentless travel and limited food.

He died on December 31, 1640, in Lalouvesc, in the Vivarais region, at the age of forty-three. According to accounts, he collapsed and died in a poor woman's home after celebrating a midnight Mass and continuing a mission retreat. He had been begging the provincial superior for permission to travel to the New World missions, particularly to the Indigenous peoples of Canada, but was turned down repeatedly due to his fragile health. The accounts of his holiness spread quickly after his death, and miracles were reported at his tomb. He was beatified in 1716 by Pope Clement XI and canonized in 1737 by Pope Clement XII.

Regis is honored as the patron saint of barbers, miners, and the unemployed, a grouping that reflects both the trades of his native region and the marginalized populations he served. His feast day is celebrated on June 16. He is remembered as a model of practical charity, and his legacy lived on through the Jesuit mission network and the many confraternities that continued his catechetical work in the French countryside. The town of Lalouvesc remains a place of pilgrimage, and his incorrupt heart is venerated in a reliquary there.

faqs.question: Who was St. John Francis Regis?
faqs.answer: St. John Francis Regis was a French Jesuit priest (1597–1640) known for his missionary preaching and charitable work among the rural poor of southern France, particularly in the regions around Toulouse, Le Velay, and Vivarais.

faqs.question: What is St. John Francis Regis the patron saint of?
faqs.answer: He is the patron saint of barbers, miners, and the unemployed, a patronage that reflects both the trades of his native region and his lifelong commitment to society's most marginalized.

faqs.question: When is St. John Francis Regis's feast day?
faqs.answer: His feast day is celebrated on June 16 in the Roman Catholic calendar.

faqs.question: Why is St. John Francis Regis associated with barbers and miners?
faqs.answer: The association with these trades comes from the trades common in the French regions where he worked, and from his practice of helping marginalized workers and the unemployed wherever he encountered them.

faqs.question: What did St. John Francis Regis do as a missionary?
faqs.answer: He walked barefoot through rural southern France, preaching parish missions, catechizing the lapsed, opposing Jansenist teaching, and organizing charitable relief for the poor, including efforts to help women in exploitative situations.

faqs.question: Where is St. John Francis Regis buried?
faqs.answer: He died at Lalouvesc in the Vivarais region of France, where his tomb became a site of pilgrimage; his heart is preserved in a reliquary in the town to this day.

biography:
John Henry Newman was born on February 21, 1801, in London, the eldest of six children. He studied at Trinity College, Oxford, where he was elected a Fellow of Oriel College in April 1822, one of the most intellectually prestigious posts at the university. He was ordained an Anglican deacon in 1824 and an Anglican priest in 1825, taking up pastoral work alongside his academic career. By the 1830s, he had become one of the central figures of the Oxford Movement, a campaign within the Church of England to recover what its members saw as the church's Catholic heritage and apostolic roots.

The Oxford Movement brought Newman into closer contact with the Church Fathers and the early Christian tradition, and over time he became increasingly convinced that the Anglican Church was not, as he had once argued, a valid branch of the one Church founded by the apostles. The decisive steps came in 1843, when he resigned the living of St Mary's, Oxford, and then in 1845, when he was received into the Roman Catholic Church. The conversion sent shockwaves through Victorian England; the clergyman who had seemed destined to lead Anglicanism into a Catholic revival instead crossed the Tiber, and old friends mourned what many saw as a tragedy.

Newman spent the years after his conversion in Rome, where he was ordained a Catholic priest and later founded the Oratory of St Philip Neri in Birmingham. In 1864, in response to accusations by the Anglican clergyman Charles Kingsley, he published his celebrated Apologia Pro Vita Sua, a spiritual autobiography widely regarded as one of the finest works of English religious prose. His Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine (1845) shaped modern thinking about how Christian truth is transmitted through history, and The Idea of a University (1852) became a classic of educational thought. He also became known for his gentle, searching style of apologetics, especially in the novel Loss and Gain (1848) and the Grammar of Assent (1870).

In 1879, Pope Leo XIII raised Newman to the College of Cardinals, the first English convert to receive that honor since the Reformation. He spent his final decades in Birmingham, where he continued writing, preaching, and advising bishops until his death on August 11, 1890. He was beatified by Pope Benedict XVI during his 2010 visit to the United Kingdom on September 19, 2010, after the Vatican recognized a miracle attributed to his intercession, and he was canonized by Pope Francis on October 13, 2019, after a second miracle was approved.

Newman's canonization took place alongside that of four other 19th- and 20th-century figures, and his feast day was set for October 9. He is widely venerated as a patron of converts, of the Personal Ordinariates erected for former Anglicans, and of intellectuals wrestling honestly with faith. His writings continue to shape Catholic thought on conscience, doctrine, and the relationship between the Church and the modern world, and he is often cited as a forerunner of key themes from the Second Vatican Council.

Newman was beatified by Pope Benedict XVI on September 19, 2010, during the pope's visit to the United Kingdom, and was canonized by Pope Francis on October 13, 2019, in Rome. His personal motto, 'Cor ad cor loquitur' ('Heart speaks to heart'), is now famously associated with his cause for canonization and with the spirituality of the Ordinariate communities.

faqs.question: Who is St. John Henry Newman?
faqs.answer: St. John Henry Newman (1801–1890) was an English theologian, author, and cardinal, widely regarded as the most influential English convert to Catholicism in the 19th century. His writings on faith, conscience, and the development of doctrine shaped Catholic thought for generations.

faqs.question: When is St. John Henry Newman's feast day?
faqs.answer: His feast day is celebrated in the Roman Catholic calendar on October 9.

faqs.question: What is St. John Henry Newman the patron saint of?
faqs.answer: He is honored as a patron of converts and of the Personal Ordinariate, the structures established to receive groups of former Anglicans into full communion with the Catholic Church.

faqs.question: Why did Newman convert to Catholicism?
faqs.answer: After years of study of the early Church Fathers, Newman concluded that the Anglican Church could not claim historical continuity with the undivided Church of the first millennium. He was received into the Roman Catholic Church in 1845.

faqs.question: What is Newman most famous for writing?
faqs.answer: Among his most influential works are the Apologia Pro Vita Sua (1864), his spiritual autobiography; An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine (1845); and The Grammar of Assent (1870), a study of how Christians come to believe.

faqs.question: Was Newman made a cardinal?
faqs.answer: Yes. In 1879, Pope Leo XIII created him a cardinal of the Catholic Church, the first English convert to receive that dignity since the Reformation.

biography: St. John I served as the Bishop of Rome and supreme pontiff of the Catholic Church from 523 until his death in 526. Elected pope shortly after the death of Pope Hormisdas, John was an Italian priest who had served in the papal administration for years before his elevation. Little is firmly known about his early life, including his precise birth date, though his career in Rome and his eventual election suggest a background rooted in the clergy of the Latin Church.

John's pontificate coincided with one of the most tense moments between the Roman See and the Ostrogothic kingdom in Italy. Theodoric the Great, the Arian Ostrogoth king, ruled Italy in uneasy cooperation with the Byzantine emperor Justin I, who was a committed Catholic. When Justin began cracking down on Arian Christians in the East, Theodoric responded by demanding that John travel to Constantinople as his ambassador, hoping to soften the emperor's stance toward Arian subjects in the West. The pope, honoring the request, set out on the journey, but he also carried a clear charge: to defend Catholic orthodoxy and the rights of the Church.

John's mission in Constantinople was diplomatically complex and theologically significant. He presided over a number of church ceremonies, and his presence in the Eastern capital became something of a public witness to Catholic unity. While there, he was reportedly honored with honors the Eastern court normally reserved for secular dignitaries, an episode that later troubled the pope. John did secure some concessions favorable to Catholics suffering under Gothic rule, but Theodoric interpreted the visit as a betrayal of his interests rather than a diplomatic success.

On his return to Italy, Theodoric had the aging pontiff arrested in Ravenna and thrown into prison. The king was enraged that the pope had not been able to persuade Justin to allow Arian worship freely within the empire and suspected John of having acted against Gothic interests. Harsh treatment in captivity, possibly combined with the privations of imprisonment and old age, led to John's death in May 526. He is recognized by the Church as a martyr, though the precise manner of his death has been debated by historians.

St. John I is traditionally listed as a martyr in the Roman Martyrology, and his feast is celebrated on May 18. He is one of only a handful of popes in Church history who died as a direct result of violence or persecution for the faith, and for that reason he is honored as a patron of popes, of voters, and of the city of Rome. His legacy is one of fidelity to orthodox Catholic teaching during a period when the Arian controversy continued to shape political and religious life across the former Roman world.

faqs.question: Who was St. John I?
faqs.answer: St. John I was the Bishop of Rome and pope from 523 to 526, remembered for his steadfast defense of Catholic doctrine during a period of tension between Rome and the Arian Ostrogoth kingdom in Italy.

faqs.question: When is St. John I's feast day?
faqs.answer: His feast day is celebrated on May 18 in the Roman Catholic calendar.

faqs.question: What is St. John I the patron saint of?
faqs.answer: He is recognized as a patron of popes, of voters, and of the city of Rome.

faqs.question: How did St. John I die?
faqs.answer: He died in May 526 after being imprisoned in Ravenna by the Arian Ostrogoth king Theodoric, whose anger over the pope's mission to Constantinople contributed to his harsh captivity and death.

faqs.question: Was St. John I a martyr?
faqs.answer: Yes, the Church lists him as a martyr in the Roman Martyrology, making him one of the few popes recognized as having died for the faith.

faqs.question: Why did St. John I travel to Constantinople?
faqs.answer: He was sent as an ambassador by the Ostrogoth king Theodoric to negotiate with the Byzantine emperor Justin I, while also defending Catholic orthodoxy and the rights of the Church in dealings with the Eastern empire.

biography:
John Nepomucene Neumann was born on March 28, 1811, in Prachatice, a small town in Bohemia (now part of the Czech Republic). He came from a German-speaking family and grew up in a region where Catholicism was practiced alongside a strong local culture. He studied for the priesthood in Prague and was ordained in 1836, but the young priest soon found that Bohemia offered little opportunity for pastoral work. The hierarchy was crowded, the diocese was under state control, and Neumann felt restless in a church where he could not fully exercise his vocation.

In 1836, encouraged by European missionaries writing home from the United States, Neumann applied to join the Redemptorists in America. He arrived in New York in 1836 with very little: by tradition, he came with only one suit and a single dollar in his pocket. He was assigned to minister to German-speaking immigrants in New York and later in Pittsburgh, and it was in this immigrant apostolate that his pastoral gifts quickly became apparent. He served as a Redemptorist missionary, spending years riding circuits on horseback through the rural countryside, hearing confessions, preaching, and serving scattered Catholic communities who rarely saw a priest. During this period he also became a naturalized American citizen in 1848.

His exceptional administrative abilities came to the attention of the U.S. bishops, and in 1852 he was unexpectedly named the fourth Bishop of Philadelphia. He was consecrated in Rome, the first bishop in the United States to receive that honor there, and returned to lead one of the largest and most diverse dioceses in the country. To serve his people, Neumann reportedly learned eight languages, a concrete expression of his conviction, captured in his famous words, 'Everyone who breathes is my neighbor.'

As bishop, Neumann set out to organize what had been a sprawling, under-instructed diocese. His most enduring achievement was the establishment of the first diocesan school system in the United States: he built or reorganized over 100 parish schools, brought religious communities of women into the city to staff them, and required Catholic children to receive regular religious instruction. He also founded an apostle band of catechists, wrote two catechisms for children, and reduced the ethnic parishes of Philadelphia into a coherent network of missions.

Neumann died on January 5, 1860, at the age of 48, after collapsing on a Philadelphia street. He was only eight years into his episcopate, yet his reforms had reshaped Catholic education in the country. He was beatified in 1963 and canonized in 1977 by Pope Paul VI, becoming the first American male to be canonized. His feast day is celebrated on January 5, the anniversary of his death, and he is venerated as the patron of sick children and of immigrants, the two groups he served most faithfully.

faqs.question: Who is St. John Neumann?
faqs.answer: St. John Neumann (1811–1860) was a Bohemian-born missionary and Redemptorist priest who became the fourth Bishop of Philadelphia. He is remembered for organizing the first diocesan school system in the United States and for his pastoral care of immigrants.

faqs.question: When is St. John Neumann's feast day?
faqs.answer: St. John Neumann's feast day is January 5, the anniversary of his death in 1860.

faqs.question: What is St. John Neumann the patron saint of?
faqs.answer: He is the patron saint of sick children and of immigrants, reflecting the two groups to whom he devoted most of his ministry.

faqs.question: What did St. John Neumann do for Catholic education?
faqs.answer: As Bishop of Philadelphia, he built or reorganized more than 100 parish schools and created the first diocesan school system in the United States, bringing religious sisters into the city to staff them.

faqs.question: Where was St. John Neumann from?
faqs.answer: He was born in Prachatice in Bohemia, in what is today the Czech Republic, and emigrated to the United States as a young priest in 1836.

faqs.question: Was St. John Neumann the first American saint?
faqs.answer: He was the first American male to be canonized, in 1977, though a number of American-born women had been canonized before him.

biography:
John of Ávila was born around 1500 in Almodóvar del Campo, in the Castilian region of Spain, into a family of converso heritage — that is, descendants of Jews who had converted to Christianity. His father was a wealthy merchant, and after his parents died when he was still young, John was raised by relatives and eventually sent to the University of Salamanca, one of the great intellectual centers of early sixteenth-century Europe. There he studied law and later arts and theology, excelling in Scripture and patristics. The intellectual rigor of Salamanca, combined with the spiritual ferment of the early Reformation era, helped shape his mind for the work ahead.

A decisive turning point came around 1526, when John redistributed a considerable inheritance to the poor and was ordained a priest. He had hoped to travel to the New World as a missionary, possibly to Mexico, but his bishop discouraged the plan, sensing that his gifts were needed at home. Instead, John returned briefly to Almodóvar, where he reportedly spent three years in a small room in his family home devoted to prayer, study, and spiritual discipline — a hidden novitiate of sorts before public ministry began.

Around 1529 he began preaching throughout the southern Spanish region of Andalusia, where his sermons drew enormous crowds of clergy and laity alike. His success provoked opposition, and he was briefly investigated by the Inquisition on suspicions drawn from jealous rivals; he was cleared. During these years he became known as the 'Apostle of Andalusia,' a title reflecting the deep religious revival his missions sparked. He was a zealous reformer of clerical life, urging priests to abandon worldliness and take seriously the call to holiness. Among those he influenced and corresponded with were figures who would themselves become saints and founders of the Spanish mystical tradition, including St. Teresa of Ávila, St. John of the Cross, St. Ignatius of Loyola (whom he briefly hosted in Manresa), and St. Francis Borgia.

Ávila's written legacy is substantial. His most famous single work, the 'Audi, filia' (Hear, O Daughter), a treatise on the spiritual life addressed to a young noblewoman, became a manual for religious formation across Catholic Europe and ran through dozens of editions. He also produced a celebrated collection of model sermons, letters of spiritual direction, and a memorable commentary on the 'Our Father.' He helped shape the work of the Council of Trent in matters of clerical reform and contributed to the founding of seminaries, including influencing the new Jesuit and Discalced Carmelite orders at decisive moments in their early growth.

After years of exhausting travel and preaching, John suffered a stroke in 1561 and settled in Montilla, where he lived the rest of his life as a semi-invalid in the house of a friend, continuing to give spiritual counsel and write. He died there on May 10, 1569, at the age of about sixty-nine. He was beatified by Pope Leo XIII in 1894 and canonized by Pope Paul VI in 1970. On October 7, 2012, Pope Benedict XVI declared him a Doctor of the Church, citing his enduring contribution to priestly formation and to the Church's understanding of the interior life. He is honored as patron of Spanish diocesan clergy and of Andalusia, and his feast is kept on May 10.

faqs.question: Who is St. John of Ávila?
faqs.answer: St. John of Ávila (c. 1500–1569) was a Spanish priest, preacher, and spiritual writer, one of the great reformers of clerical life in sixteenth-century Spain. He is often called the 'Apostle of Andalusia' for his missionary preaching there.

faqs.question: When is St. John of Ávila's feast day?
faqs.answer: His feast day is celebrated on May 10, the date of his death in 1569.

faqs.question: What is St. John of Ávila the patron saint of?
faqs.answer: He is the patron of Spanish diocesan clergy and of Andalusia, the southern region of Spain where he did most of his preaching.

faqs.question: When was St. John of Ávila declared a Doctor of the Church?
faqs.answer: Pope Benedict XVI declared him a Doctor of the Church on October 7, 2012, in recognition of his writings on the spiritual life and priestly formation.

faqs.question: What is St. John of Ávila known for?
faqs.answer: He is known for his powerful preaching in Andalusia, his treatise 'Audi, filia' (Hear, O Daughter), and his spiritual guidance of saints including St. Teresa of Ávila, St. John of the Cross, and St. Francis Borgia.

faqs.question: Why is he called the 'Apostle of Andalusia'?
faqs.answer: The title reflects the impact of his years of itinerant preaching across southern Spain beginning in the late 1520s, which sparked a notable religious revival among clergy and laity alike.

biography: John of Beverley was an Anglo-Saxon bishop and monastic founder whose ministry shaped the early church in northern England. The details of his birth and early family life are not well documented, and the exact dates of his birth and death remain uncertain. He is generally placed in the early to mid-eighth century, during the period when the Christian faith was being firmly established among the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms. He is known to have been educated at Canterbury under Archbishop Theodore of Tarsus, the Greek-born scholar whose influence on English church life and learning was immense, and to have later served as a deacon and priest in the kingdom of Northumbria.

John rose to become Bishop of Hexham (sometimes called Hagustald) in the early eighth century, succeeding Bishop Acca in that see. He later transferred to the bishopric of York, succeeding Bishop Wilfrid II, who had himself succeeded the great Wilfrid. According to Bede, John was a man of learning and pastoral concern, qualities that would have been especially valued in a church still consolidating its monastic and missionary identity after the Synod of Whitby and the controversies that surrounded it. He is credited with founding or significantly developing a monastery at a place that came to be called Beverley, in what is now the East Riding of Yorkshire, on land said to have been given to him by a local lord whom he had healed.

Among the traditions associated with John of Beverley is the story that the famous historian and monk Bede was ordained to the priesthood by him, and that Bede was deeply devoted to his memory. Bede recorded an account of John teaching a young deaf student at his monastery, who, after instruction and prayer, recovered his hearing and went on to become learned in Latin and Greek. This story has often been cited as a witness to John's care for education and for those with disabilities. The exact historical reliability of individual miracle accounts is difficult to verify, but the underlying reputation of John as a pastor concerned with both learning and the relief of human suffering is consistent with what Bede himself reports of him.

John is said to have retired to his monastery at Beverley before his death, and the community there grew in importance after his burial, becoming a significant center of pilgrimage and learning in medieval England. His remains were later translated, or moved, to a more prominent shrine, and the monastery of Beverley became one of the wealthiest and most influential in northern England before the Norman Conquest and the eventual dissolution of the monasteries. In 1037 his relics were translated to a new resting place, an event recorded in liturgical sources of the period, though specific details vary.

His feast day is celebrated on May 7 in the Roman calendar, and he is honored as a patron of the city and archdiocese of York. The church in England and in the wider Communion of Saints has long invoked him as a model of pastoral care, learning, and faithful governance. His legacy endures especially in the history of York and of Beverley itself, where the minister of Beverley and other local landmarks preserve the memory of an early English bishop who combined contemplation with the practical work of building up the Christian community.

faqs.question: Who is Saint John of Beverley?
faqs.answer: Saint John of Beverley was an eighth-century Anglo-Saxon bishop who served as Bishop of Hexham and later Bishop of York, and is best known for founding the monastery at Beverley in northern England.

faqs.question: When is Saint John of Beverley's feast day?
faqs.answer: His feast day is May 7 in the Roman Catholic calendar.

faqs.question: What is Saint John of Beverley the patron saint of?
faqs.answer: He is honored as a patron of York, England, and is also invoked by some as a patron of education and the healing of those with hearing difficulties.

faqs.question: What is Saint John of Beverley known for?
faqs.answer: He is known for his work as a bishop, his founding of the monastery at Beverley, and his concern for education and pastoral care, including a tradition recorded by Bede of him teaching a deaf student who recovered his hearing through prayer.

faqs.question: Did Saint John of Beverley have a connection to the Venerable Bede?
faqs.answer: Yes, Bede records that he was ordained a priest by John of Beverley, and Bede devoted a chapter of his Historia Ecclesiastica to John's life, miracles, and pastoral character.

faqs.question: Where is Saint John of Beverley buried?
faqs.answer: He was buried at his monastery at Beverley in the East Riding of Yorkshire, and his remains were later translated to a more prominent shrine within the monastery, which became an important center of medieval pilgrimage.

biography: John of Capistrano was born in 1386 in Capistrano, in the Abruzzi region of southern Italy. The son of a former knight who had been briefly imprisoned, he received a solid education in law and went on to serve as a magistrate in the Kingdom of Naples. His early life was that of an ambitious young man climbing the ranks of civil administration, but it took a dramatic turn when he was sent as an envoy to King Ladislaus of Naples. Imprisoned on suspicion of conspiracy, he reportedly experienced a spiritual crisis during his captivity. Upon his release, John renounced his career and his marriage, and entered the Franciscan Order of Friars Minor, being ordained in 1420.

His entry into the Franciscans brought him under the influence of the Observant branch's reform movement, and he was soon drawn into collaboration with the great Franciscan preacher Bernardine of Siena. Following Bernardine's death in 1444, John of Capistrano emerged as one of the most effective itinerant preachers of fifteenth-century Europe. He traveled extensively through Italy, Germany, Bohemia, Poland, and the Balkans, drawing enormous crowds with his powerful, sometimes harsh preaching on sin, penance, and the call to reform. He was also a skilled administrator, serving as papal inquisitor and as vicar general of the Observant Franciscans, and he helped found or reorganize numerous Franciscan communities, particularly in Central Europe. He was active in the 1452 debate at the court of Frederick III in Wiener Neustadt, defending Jewish communities against false blood libels.

In his sixties, John turned his energies toward confronting the military threat of the Ottoman Empire. He was the chief preacher of the Crusade proclaimed by Pope Callixtus III, traveling through Hungary, Serbia, and beyond to rally support, organize supplies, and raise funds. In the summer of 1456, he joined the defense of Belgrade alongside the Hungarian general John Hunyadi, who led the actual military operation. The Ottoman forces were repulsed on July 14, 1456, in a battle often credited with checking Ottoman expansion into Central Europe for decades. Worn down by age, privation, and the rigors of his campaign, John died on October 23, 1456, in the town of Sremski Karlovci (Ilok), in present-day Serbia.

He was canonized by Pope Callixtus III on August 16, 1456 — the same year as his death. While he is sometimes remembered as a kind of 'second founder' of the Franciscan Observants, he is more precisely recognized in Franciscan tradition as one of the four great evangelical doctors (doctores evangelici) alongside Bonaventure, Anthony of Padua, and Lawrence of Brindisi. He is the patron saint of military chaplains, jurists, and the city of Belgrade, and his feast is kept on October 23.

faqs.question: Who was St. John of Capistrano?
faqs.answer: St. John of Capistrano (1386–1456) was an Italian Franciscan friar and itinerant preacher, famous for his powerful preaching across Europe and for inspiring the Christian defense of Belgrade against the Ottomans in 1456.

faqs.question: When is St. John of Capistrano's feast day?
faqs.answer: His feast day is celebrated on October 23, the anniversary of his death in 1456.

faqs.question: What is St. John of Capistrano the patron saint of?
faqs.answer: He is a patron saint of military chaplains, jurists, and the city of Belgrade.

faqs.question: What did St. John of Capistrano do?
faqs.answer: He preached throughout Europe, helped reform and reorganize the Franciscan Observants, served as a papal inquisitor, and in his final years was the chief preacher of the 1456 Crusade, helping to rally the defense of Belgrade against the Ottoman army.

faqs.question: Where was John of Capistrano from?
faqs.answer: He was born in Capistrano, in the Abruzzi region of southern Italy, and spent much of his preaching career traveling across the Italian peninsula and into Central and Eastern Europe.

faqs.question: Was John of Capistrano a Doctor of the Church?
faqs.answer: No — he is not one of the official Doctors of the Church, but he is honored within the Franciscan tradition as one of the four great evangelical doctors (doctores evangelici), alongside St. Bonaventure, St. Anthony of Padua, and St. Lawrence of Brindisi.

biography:
John of Damascus was born around 676 in Damascus, then under Umayyad Muslim rule. His family, though Christian, was prominent and well-placed in the caliphate's administration, which is likely how the young John came to serve as a senior financial official — sometimes described as chief treasurer — in the court of the caliph. Educated in the intellectual traditions of the region, he became one of the most learned Christian figures of his era, even as he lived as a subject of an Islamic government. His own later writings reflect both this classical formation and a deep grounding in Scripture and the Greek Church Fathers.

Around the age of 40, John gave up his position at court and entered the Monastery of Mar Saba in the Judean desert, near Jerusalem. The traditional account holds that he was tonsured along with the young orphan whom he had adopted and was raising as a companion, and that the boy's apparent death soon after was taken by John as a sign confirming his monastic calling. In the monastery he lived a strict life of prayer, study, and writing, producing sermons, hymns, and the major treatises that would shape Eastern Christian theology for centuries.

John is best remembered for his defense of sacred images during the Iconoclast Controversy. When the Byzantine Emperor Leo III began ordering the destruction of icons in the 720s and 730s, John — safely outside the emperor's reach in the Umayyad caliphate — wrote three treatises known collectively as the Apologetic Treatises against those who Decry Holy Images. In these works he distinguished veneration (dulia) from worship (latria), argued that matter itself is good because created by God, and laid out a theology of images that became foundational for the Orthodox tradition and for the later Catholic position. The most famous of his images, the words "I do not worship matter, but the Creator of matter," captures the core of his argument.

His major dogmatic work, The Fount of Knowledge, gathered patristic thought into a single synthesis and remained a standard theological textbook in the East for generations. He is also credited with codifying Byzantine chant and composing a rich body of liturgical poetry still sung in Eastern Christian churches, most notably the canon for the Nativity in the voice of the Magi and the paschal canon "The golden singing." By the time of his death in 749, he had become the principal Eastern voice for the legitimacy of holy icons — a position eventually affirmed at the Second Council of Nicaea in 787.

John of Damascus is honored as the last of the great Church Fathers of the undivided tradition. He was declared a Doctor of the Church by Pope Leo XIII in the late 19th century (most commonly cited as 1890), making him one of only a handful of Eastern Christians to receive the title. He is traditionally venerated on December 4. Over the centuries his reputation as a theologian, hymnographer, and defender of icons has only grown, and he is regarded as a patron of icon painters, pharmacists, and theology students — the last patronage, fittingly, reflecting his enduring influence on Christian intellectual life.

faqs.question: Who is St. John of Damascus?
faqs.answer: St. John of Damascus (c. 676–749) was a Syrian Christian monk, priest, and theologian, widely regarded as the last of the Church Fathers. He is best known for defending the veneration of icons during the Iconoclast Controversy and for his theological and liturgical writings, including The Fount of Knowledge.

faqs.question: When is St. John of Damascus's feast day?
faqs.answer: St. John of Damascus is commemorated on December 4 in the Roman Catholic calendar. Eastern Christian traditions may also celebrate him on other dates.

faqs.question: What is St. John of Damascus the patron saint of?

faqs.question: Why is St. John of Damascus important for icons?

faqs.question: What did St. John of Damascus do before becoming a monk?
